error: UnicodeEncodeError('utf-8', '{"elapsed_ms": 48646.0, "run_id": "run-q2013", "event": "fetch.raw", "url": "https://viajacongus.com/en/laos/si-phan-don/", "content": "Jump to what you need\\n\\n📍Region\\n\\nSi Phan Don, the \'4000 islands\', is the stretch of the Mekong where the river, shortly before the Cambodian border, widens to as much as 14 km and breaks up into a maze of islands, islets and sandbanks, many of which disappear when the monsoon floods arrive. It lies at the far south of Laos, in Champasak province, about 150 km from Pakse. It is one of the most peaceful and beautiful parts of the country: hammocks, sunsets, rice paddies, thundering waterfalls and the rare Irrawaddy dolphins. The main islands for travellers are Don Khong (the largest), Don Det and Don Khon.\\n\\n📌Best time to go\\n\\nThe best season is the dry season, from November to February, with pleasant weather, clear skies and the river at its lowest, ideal for cycling and for seeing the waterfalls and the dolphins. March to May is very hot. In the rainy season (June to October) the Mekong rises enormously, the waterfalls (Khone Phapheng, Li Phi) are at their most spectacular and the landscape turns green, but the humid heat and the mosquitoes increase. For dolphin spotting, the dry season (December to May) gives better chances because the water level is low.\\n\\n📌Suggested days\\n\\n2 or 3 days are enough to enjoy it properly: time to relax in a hammock, cycle around Don Det and Don Khon across the old French bridge, see the Li Phi (Somphamit) and Khone Phapheng waterfalls, and head out by boat to look for the Irrawaddy dolphins. Don Khong, bigger and quieter, adds rural life. It\'s a place to slow down: many people come for two nights and stay a week. If you\'re short on time, give it at least two nights.\\n\\n📌Getting there\\n\\nThe overland gateway is Ban Nakasang, a village on Route 13 about 150 km from Pakse, with a boat landing. From Pakse there are minivans and local buses; from Cambodia (Nong Nok Khiene/Trapeang Kriel border crossing), international buses to and from Siem Reap and Phnom Penh. At Nakasang you take the boat to Don Det or Don Khon (about 20-30 min). Don Khong has a separate access, via a bridge from Route 13. There\'s no airport nearby; the most useful one is Pakse. The Laos-China railway doesn\'t reach the south.\\n\\n📌Getting around\\n\\nBetween the islands and from the mainland, everything goes by boat: flat-bottomed motorboats that cross the Mekong between Nakasang, Don Det, Don Khon and Don Khong. On the islands themselves, the star way to get around is the bicycle (rented for a few thousand kip) or the motorbike; Don Det and Don Khon are linked by a French-era pedestrian/cycle bridge, so you can explore them together. To see the dolphins or the more remote waterfalls you hire boats with local boatmen. There are no cars and no traffic: that\'s part of the charm.\\n\\n📌Language and currency\\n\\nThe official language is Lao; in the islands\' guesthouses, restaurants and agencies a fair amount of English is spoken thanks to backpacker tourism. The currency is the Lao kip (LAK); because of devaluation it\'s worth checking the exchange rate (it was around 21,000-22,000 per dollar in 2026). Everything is paid in kip, in cash (boats, waterfall entry, bikes, food, accommodation). There\'s the odd ATM in Nakasang and on the larger islands, but they don\'t always work: withdraw enough cash in Pakse before you come, because running out of money on the islands is a real problem.\\n\\n💱 LAK exchange rate\\n\\n🇺🇸 1 USD 22,442 LAK\\n\\n🇪🇺 1 EUR 25,105 LAK\\n\\n🇬🇧 1 GBP 29,996 LAK\\n\\n🇨🇦 1 CAD 15,838 LAK\\n\\n🇯🇵 1 JPY 142 LAK\\n\\nLive rate · open.er-api.com\\n\\n🌤️ Weather in Si Phan Don (4000 Islands)\\n\\n26°Thunderstorm ⛈️\\n\\nWed⛈️23° / **32°**\\n\\nThu\udf26️23° / **32°**\\n\\nFri\udf26️24° / **32°**\\n\\nLive · open-meteo.com\\n\\nSi Phan Don, the \'4000 islands\', is the perfect finale to a trip through southern Laos: the place where the mighty Mekong, tired after crossing half a continent, widens, branches out and dissolves into a maze of islands, islets and sandbanks before rushing on into Cambodia. It\'s a world of water and calm, with no cars and no hurry, where time is set by the sun, the hammocks and the slow passing of the boats. Many travellers arrive planning to stay two days and end up giving in to its rhythm for a week.\\n\\nBut Si Phan Don isn\'t just hammocks and sunsets. Here the Mekong hides some major surprises: the Khone Phapheng Falls, the largest by volume in Southeast Asia, a roaring wall of water; the Li Phi (Somphamit) rapids, spectacular when the river is high; the rare and endangered Irrawaddy dolphins, which can be spotted in a stretch of the river near the border; and even the ruins of an old French railway, the only one Laos ever had, built to get around the falls. All of it set among rice paddies, palm trees and fishing villages.\\n\\nThis guide lays out the visit from a practical angle: which islands to choose (Don Det, Don Khon, Don Khong), what to see and do, how to get there from Pakse or from Cambodia, how to get around by boat and bike, what things cost, and where to eat and sleep. The history of the Mekong, the colonial railway and the dolphins is on our history page. Si Phan Don is the ideal place to end your trip slowly, with your feet in the river.\\n\\n## 📖 History of Si Phan Don (4000 Islands)\\n\\nThe 4000 islands are a phenomenon of the lower Mekong: here the river, before entering Cambodia, widens and runs into a rocky ledge that forms the Khone Phapheng Falls, the largest by volume in Southeast Asia and impassable for boats. That natural barrier shaped the area\'s history. In the late 19th century, when France dreamed of using the Mekong as a trade route to China, the falls thwarted the plan: to get around them, colonial engineers built a small narrow-gauge railway in the early 20th century between the islands of Don Det and Don Khon — the only railway Laos ever had — with a bridge that still links the two islands. The area has always been home to Lao fishermen, and its waters shelter the river\'s last Irrawaddy dolphins, now critically endangered. The history of the Mekong, the French railway and the dolphins is on our history page.\\n\\n[Read the full history ↓](https://viajacongus.com/en/laos/si-phan-don/#historia)\\n\\n## 🏛️ Si Phan Don (4000 Islands) is in South (Mekong, coffee and islands)\\n\\nThe deep south of Laos: the old Kingdom of Champasak and its Khmer temple of Wat Phou, a World Heritage Site; the cool Bolaven Plateau, home of Lao coffee since French times; and the 4000 Islands, where the Mekong scatters before reaching Cambodia.\\n\\n[Read the history of South (Mekong, coffee and islands) →](https://viajacongus.com/en/laos/historia/#prov-sur-mekong-cafe-islas)\\n\\n## 🚌 How to get there and distances\\n\\n### Getting around\\n\\nBoat between islands and to the mainland\\n\\nPrice\\n\\nNakasang ↔ Don Det/Don Khon ~15.000-20.000 kip per person in a group; short crossings cheaper, 2026\\n\\nNotes\\n\\nThe essential transport on the islands. Boats leave once they fill up; in a group it\'s cheaper per head. Agree on the price and the return time before getting on\\n\\nBicycle\\n\\n~10.000-20.000 kip/day, 2026\\n\\nNotes\\n\\nThe star way to get around the islands. hammock free at your bungalow, 2026 | An afternoon | Guesthouses and riverside bars |\\n\\n🔄 updated monthly Official / reference values · double-check when buying\\n\\n## 🗺️ What to do\\n\\n1\\n\\nKhone Phapheng Falls\\n\\nThe largest waterfall by volume in Southeast Asia: a thundering wall of Mekong water just before Cambodia.\\n\\nRead more ↓\\nKhone Phapheng is the natural jewel of Si Phan Don and one of the most impressive waterfalls in Asia. It isn\'t the tallest — its drop is modest in height — but it is the largest by volume in Southeast Asia: when the monsoon floods come, a colossal volume of Mekong water plunges over a series of rapids and rocky drops, forming a roaring wall of foam you can hear from far away. This ledge is what makes the Mekong unnavigable along this stretch, and what dashed the colonial dream of using the river as a route to China. The site has viewpoints, walkways and a park, on the mainland side (not on the backpacker islands), and is usually visited on an excursion. The sight of the entire river pouring between the rocks, especially at high water, is breathtaking. There are also food stalls and good views towards the Cambodian border. Getting there: on the mainland, near Ban Nakasang; reached by tour, motorbike or tuk-tuk (it\'s not on Don Det/Don Khon). Best time: during and after the rains (August-October) for maximum flow; impressive all year round. Tips: combine it with your visit to the islands or stop on the way to/from the border; bring water and a hat; and don\'t try to get too close to the water, as the current is lethal.\\n\\nℹ️ Distance: On the mainland, near Nakasang; not on Don Det/Don Khon · Best time: After the rains (Aug-Oct) for maximum flow · Admission: ~30.000-55.000 kip; open ~8:00-18:00 (verified July 2026) · Duration: 1 to 2 hours\\n\\n2\\n\\nLi Phi Falls (Somphamit)\\n\\nA spectacular stretch of rapids and cascades on Don Khon island, with a legend of a \'spirit trap\'.\\n\\nRead more ↓\\nThe Li Phi Falls, also called Somphamit, are on Don Khon island and are one of the big draws of the 4000 islands, easier to reach than Khone Phapheng if you\'re staying on Don Det or Don Khon. They aren\'t a single drop but a chaotic, powerful jumble of rapids, channels and cascades where the Mekong forces its way between rocks and islets, especially furious when the river is high. The name \'Li Phi\' is sometimes translated as \'spirit trap\': local tradition says the souls of the dead and evil spirits get caught among these rapids. There are walkways and viewpoints to see them, and nearby a river beach to relax on in the dry season (carefully, as the current is treacherous). It\'s a classic stop on the bike ride around Don Khon. Getting there: on Don Khon, reached by boat and then by bike from Don Det across the old French bridge. Best time: after the rains for the flow; the dry season is better for the beach. Tips: the Li Phi ticket usually includes crossing the bridge between the islands; wear sturdy shoes, don\'t go into the water near the rapids, and carry on to the southern tip of Don Khon to look for dolphins.\\n\\nℹ️ Distance: Don Khon island; by bike from Don Det across the French bridge · Best time: After the rains for the flow; dry season for the beach · Admission: ~35.000 kip (usually includes crossing the Don Det-Don Khon bridge) (verified July 2026) · Duration: 1 to 2 hours\\n\\n3\\n\\nIrrawaddy dolphins\\n\\nThe Mekong\'s rare and endangered river dolphins, seen in a stretch near the Cambodian border.\\n\\nRead more ↓\\nOne of the great treasures of Si Phan Don is the Irrawaddy dolphin, a species of river dolphin with a rounded head and no \'beak\', now critically endangered. Only a tiny population survives in the Mekong, concentrated in a deep stretch of the river on the Laos-Cambodia border, near the southern tip of Don Khon. Seeing them, even from a distance and for a few seconds as they surface to breathe, is a moving and bittersweet experience, given how threatened they are. Trips leave by boat from the southern tip of Don Khon (Ban Hang Khon area): local boatmen take visitors to the pool where the dolphins usually gather and wait for them to appear. Sightings aren\'t guaranteed, but the odds are good, especially in the dry season, when the water level drops. It\'s essential to choose responsible boatmen who keep their distance and don\'t harass the animals. Getting there: by bike to the southern tip of Don Khon and then by boat with a local boatman. Best time: dry season (December-May), with the river lower, for better sightings. Tips: go early in the morning or at sunset (when the dolphins are most active), bring binoculars if you have them, don\'t expect an aquarium-style show (they\'re wild and scarce animals), and support the boatmen who look after the dolphins.\\n\\nℹ️ Distance: Southern tip of Don Khon (Ban Hang Khon), Cambodian border · Best time: Dry season (Dec-May), with the river lower · Admission: Dolphin-watching boat ~100.000 kip per person (depending on group) (verified July 2026) · Duration: 1 to 2 hours\\n\\n4\\n\\nThe remains of the only train Laos ever had, with its colonial bridge that still links the two backpacker islands.\\n\\nRead more ↓\\nBetween the islands of Don Det and Don Khon lies a unique historical curiosity: the remains of the only railway Laos ever had. In the early 20th century the French, unable to get boats past the Mekong falls, built a small narrow-gauge railway of about 7 km across both islands, to move goods and even dismantled boats from one side of the rapids to the other. It ran for decades and was key to colonial trade on the lower Mekong. What\'s left of the railway is the old track bed, the odd rusty locomotive kept as a monument and, above all, the concrete bridge linking Don Det with Don Khon, now a pedestrian and cycle crossing and a symbol of the islands. Cycling across it, with the Mekong rushing below, is one of the classic moments of a visit. It\'s a tangible window onto the ambition — and the frustration — of the French colonial project on the river. Getting there: the bridge links Don Det and Don Khon; cross on foot or by bike. Best time: all year round, best in the morning light or at sunset. Tips: the bridge toll is usually included in the Li Phi ticket; look out for the remains of the locomotive and the old piers; and make the most of it by cycling the whole \'railway route\' between the two islands.\\n\\nℹ️ Distance: Between Don Det and Don Khon; central bridge · Best time: All year round; morning or sunset · Admission: Bridge toll ~ included in the Li Phi ticket (~35.000 kip) (verified July 2026) · Duration: Part of the bike ride\\n\\n5\\n\\nDon Khong, the big quiet island\\n\\nThe largest island in Si Phan Don, more rural and less backpacker-oriented, ideal for seeing Lao riverside life.\\n\\nRead more ↓\\nDon Khong is the largest of the 4000 islands and shows a different side of Si Phan Don: bigger, more populated and far less backpacker-oriented than Don Det. It\'s an island of villages, rice paddies, Buddhist temples and rural Lao life, with an unhurried, authentic pace, ideal if you\'re after peace and quiet and a feel for everyday life in the south, away from Don Det\'s bar scene. It\'s great to explore by bike or motorbike: roads between rice fields, fishing villages, wats with monks, morning markets and good spots to watch the sunset over the Mekong. A bridge connects it to Route 13 on the mainland, making it easier to reach with your own transport. It\'s a perfect base for a more serene version of the islands. Getting there: by bridge from Route 13, or by boat; about 120-130 km from Pakse. Best time: dry season for comfortable cycling. Tips: rent a bike or motorbike to loop around the island; visit the temples and the morning market in Muang Khong; and stay at least one night to soak up the calm pace, very different from Don Det\'s.\\n\\nℹ️ Distance: ~120-130 km from Pakse; connected by bridge to Route 13 · Best time: Dry season for cycling · Admission: Free; bike rental ~10.000-20.000 kip/day, motorbike ~50.000-80.000 kip/day (verified July 2026) · Duration: Half a day to an overnight stay\\n\\n6\\n\\nBike rides, kayaking and sunsets\\n\\nThe soul of Si Phan Don: cycling among rice paddies, paddling through the Mekong\'s channels and watching the sun go down from a hammock.\\n\\nRead more ↓\\nBeyond the waterfalls and the dolphins, the best \'attraction\' of the 4000 islands is its pace. The top activity is cycling aimlessly around Don Det and Don Khon: dirt tracks between rice paddies, palm trees and villages, crossing the French bridge, stopping for a swim or a drink with a river view. In a few hours you can loop around both islands, and every bend offers a Mekong postcard. The water invites you to do more: kayak trips explore the channels between the islands, with stops at waterfalls and at the dolphin pool, combining paddling, nature and the odd gentle rapid. And at the end of the day comes the big free show: sunset over the Mekong, which turns everything orange when seen from the hammocks of the bungalows or from a riverside bar. It\'s the moment that defines Si Phan Don. Getting there: bikes and kayak trips are rented/booked on Don Det and Don Khon. Best time: dry season for cycling and kayaking; sunsets are good all year round. Tips: start your bike ride early or late in the afternoon because of the heat; pick a west-facing bungalow or bar for the sunset; and don\'t overfill your schedule: the plan here is precisely to have no plan.\\n\\nℹ️ Distance: Don Det and Don Khon; surrounding Mekong channels · Best time: Dry season for bike/kayak; sunsets all year round · Admission: Bike ~10.000-20.000 kip/day; kayak trip ~150.000-250.000 kip per person (verified July 2026) · Duration: A few hours to a full day\\n\\n## 🛡️ Getting sick far from home shouldn\'t cost you thousands of USD\\n\\nAbroad, getting sick is more than a bad day. The bungalows and bars on Don Det and Don Khon serve Lao food (laap, Mekong fish, curry, sticky rice) and backpacker dishes (sandwiches, pasta, breakfasts), with the best views of the river and the sunset\\n\\nLocal food and stalls\\n\\nOptions / signature dish\\n\\nDishes 10.000-35.000 kip, 2026. Book one with a river view\\n\\nBackpacker (Don Det guesthouses)\\n\\nRecommended options\\n\\nBasic bungalow ~40.000-120.000 kip; hostel dorm ~40.000-80.000 kip, 2026. Don Det is backpacker heaven: simple bungalows and hostels with hammocks and a social vibe, dirt cheap. Most of the options are on the \'sunrise\' and \'sunset\' sides. Payment is in cash\\n\\nRural and quiet (Don Khong)\\n\\nRecommended options\\n\\n~15-45 USD per night, 2026. Guesthouses and small hotels in Muang Khong and the villages of Don Khong, ideal for a calmer, more authentic experience among rice paddies and temples, far from the bustle of Don Det\\n\\n## More places in Laos\\n\\n## ❓ Frequently asked questions\\n\\nHow many days should I stay in the 4000 Islands?+\\nIdeally 2 or 3 days: enough to relax, cycle around Don Det and Don Khon across the French bridge, see the Li Phi and Khone Phapheng falls and head out by boat to look for the dolphins. But it\'s a place that hooks you: plenty of people come for two nights and stay a week, won over by its slow pace. If you\'re short on time, give it at least two nights; anything less doesn\'t do it justice.\\n\\nWhich island should I choose: Don Det, Don Khon or Don Khong?+\\nDon Det is the most backpacker-oriented and lively, with cheap bungalows, bars and a social vibe; ideal if you want company and low-key partying. Don Khon, linked to Don Det by the French bridge, is more peaceful and has the Li Phi falls and access to the dolphins. Don Khong is the largest, most rural and authentic, perfect for switching off among rice paddies and temples. Many people stay on Don Det or Don Khon and visit the rest by bike and boat.\\n\\nHow do I get to Si Phan Don?+\\nThe overland gateway is Ban Nakasang, on Route 13 about 150 km from Pakse (3-4 h by minivan or bus), where you take the boat to Don Det or Don Khon (20-30 min). From Cambodia, international buses cross the Nong Nok Khiene border to/from Siem Reap and Phnom Penh. Don Khong has its own bridge from Route 13. There\'s no airport nearby (the most useful is Pakse) and the Laos-China railway doesn\'t reach the south.\\n\\nCan you see the Irrawaddy dolphins? Is it worth it?+\\nYes, you can, although it isn\'t guaranteed and they are few: a tiny, highly endangered population survives in a stretch of the Mekong near the Cambodian border (the southern tip of Don Khon). The trip is by boat and your chances are good, especially in the dry season (December-May). Don\'t expect an aquarium show: these are wild animals that surface for a few seconds to breathe. Choose responsible boatmen who keep their distance and don\'t harass them.\\n\\nWhen is the best time to visit?+\\nThe dry season (November to February) is the most comfortable: good weather and clear skies, ideal for cycling and for seeing the dolphins (the lower river helps). March to May is very hot. In the rainy season (June to October) the Mekong rises and the falls (Khone Phapheng, Li Phi) are spectacular, but the humid heat and the mosquitoes increase. To combine weather, waterfalls and dolphins, aim for November-December.\\n\\nAre there ATMs and wifi on the islands?+\\nFew, and not always reliable. There\'s the odd ATM in Nakasang and on the bigger islands, but they often fail or run out of cash, so withdraw enough kip in Pakse before you come; running out of money on the islands is a real problem. Wifi and mobile signal exist but are limited: that\'s part of Si Phan Don\'s disconnected charm. Everything is paid in cash (boats, admission, bikes, food, accommodation).\\n\\n## 📖 History of Si Phan Don (4000 Islands)\\n\\nOrigins, formation and what the sources say.\\n\\n### Where the great river breaks into a thousand pieces\\n\\nThere is a place, at the far southern tip of Laos, where the Mekong seems to grow tired. After travelling almost five thousand kilometres from the heights of Tibet, through China, Myanmar, Thailand and half of Laos, the great river reaches a vast plain and, just before entering Cambodia, widens to fourteen kilometres and dissolves into a maze of islands, islets, channels and sandbanks. The Lao people named it with poetic simplicity: Si Phan Don, the \'four thousand islands\'.\\n\\nThe number isn\'t literal —many of those \'islands\' are little more than sandbanks that appear and disappear with the pulse of the monsoon—, but the image is spot on. In the dry season, the landscape is a jigsaw of land between calm channels; when the rains swell the river, the water rises several metres and swallows a good part of the islets, leaving only the larger islands, such as Don Khong, Don Det and Don Khon.\\n\\nThis widening is no accident: here the Mekong runs into a geological threshold, a barrier of rock that creates one of the river\'s most impressive sights, the Khone Falls. That natural feature, which shapes the landscape of the 4000 Islands, would also shape their history: the barrier no boat could cross, which thwarted one of the great colonial dreams of the 19th century.\\n\\n### The falls that blocked the road to China\\n\\nThe Khone Falls —of which Khone Phapheng is the most spectacular— are the largest waterfall by volume in Southeast Asia. What impresses is not their height but their sheer volume: in flood season, a colossal flow from the whole Mekong hurls itself between the rocks in a fury of foam you can hear kilometres away. For nature, they are a wonder. For navigation, they were for centuries an impassable barrier.\\n\\nAnd that is the key to their history. In the late 19th century, as France was building its empire in Indochina, explorers and merchants dreamed of using the Mekong as a great river highway linking Saigon with the interior of China, opening up an immense market. The French expedition that travelled up the river in the 1860s pinned all its hopes on that route. But on arriving here, at the Khone Falls, the dream came crashing down: no boat could get past that wall of water and rock. The Mekong, it turned out, was not navigable from end to end.\\n\\nThat discovery changed the history of the region. With a continuous river route ruled out, France had to find a way around the falls to at least keep trade going on the lower Mekong. The solution colonial engineers came up with is one of the most surprising historical curiosities in Laos: building a railway in the middle of the jungle and the islands.\\n\\n### Laos\'s only train: a railway between islands\\n\\nIn the early 20th century, to get around the obstacle of the falls, the French did something unusual: they built a narrow-gauge railway of about seven kilometres across the islands of Don Det and Don Khon, linking the navigable stretches of the Mekong above and below the rapids. It was the first and only railway Laos had in its entire history.\\n\\nThe system was ingenious and laborious: boats came up the river to one end, the cargo was unloaded —and sometimes entire vessels were taken apart—, carried by train across the islands to the other end, and there loaded again onto boats that continued downstream or upstream. Piers, embankments and the concrete bridge that still links Don Det with Don Khon were built, and small locomotives ran along those tracks for decades.\\n\\nThe railway operated until the mid-20th century, when the decline of river trade, the Second World War and the Indochina wars left it out of use. Today, traces remain: the embankment turned into a path, an old rusty locomotive or two displayed as monuments and, above all, the bridge, now a crossing for bicycles and pedestrians and a symbol of the islands. Cycling across it, with the Mekong rushing below, is touching first-hand the ambition and the frustration of the French colonial project on the river.\\n\\n### The last dolphins of the Mekong\\n\\nIn the deep waters of the Mekong, near the border between Laos and Cambodia, one of the river\'s rarest and most endearing animals survives: the Irrawaddy dolphin. It is a river dolphin with a rounded head, without the \'beak\' of marine dolphins, which for centuries lived alongside the fishermen of the lower Mekong and held a place in their beliefs and legends, which regarded it as an almost sacred animal, the reincarnation of benevolent spirits.\\n\\nToday, however, these dolphins are on the brink of extinction in the Mekong. Of the large populations of the past, only a handful of individuals remain, concentrated in a few deep pools around the 4000 Islands and the border stretch with Cambodia. The causes of their decline are many and sobering: gillnet fishing, in which they get trapped and drown; the use of explosives and poison for fishing; the degradation of the river; and, more recently, the impact of the large hydroelectric dams that fragment and alter their habitat.\\n\\nWatching one of these dolphins surface to breathe, even for just a few seconds, is a moving and bittersweet experience: you are looking at a survivor of a species that may not see many more decades in the Mekong. Its fate sums up the tensions running through the whole river: between development and conservation, between human needs and the survival of a unique ecosystem. The dolphins of Si Phan Don are a treasure and, at the same time, a warning.\\n\\n### The 4000 Islands today: the art of doing nothing\\n\\nAfter the end of colonial river trade and the decades of war and isolation Laos went through in the 20th century, the 4000 Islands remained what they had always been beneath the surface of the French project: a world of Lao fishermen and rice farmers, living to the rhythm of the Mekong. That slow, almost suspended rhythm is today their greatest attraction for visitors.\\n\\nSince the 1990s and 2000s, as Laos opened up to tourism, Si Phan Don —and Don Det in particular— became a destination loved by backpackers from all over the world, drawn by its cheap bungalows over the river, its hammocks, its sunsets and its total absence of hurry. Alongside that laid-back tourism, the islands offer their unique heritage: the thundering falls, the ruins of the old railway, the Li Phi rapids and the fragile thrill of looking for dolphins.\\n\\nThe great challenge of the present is balance. The 4000 Islands live, like the whole lower Mekong, under the threat of large dams upstream and hydroelectric projects, which alter the pulse of the river on which the fish, the dolphins, the rice paddies and the island landscape itself depend. For now, Si Phan Don is still one of the most peaceful and beautiful corners of Southeast Asia: a place where the great river opens up, breathes and teaches anyone willing to go with the flow the
